finding: The round-2 finding on a wip task under a block that appears later named two outcomes: tp next and tp resume keep offering the WIP task, or tp resume offers no implement unit and the WIP task stalls. The repair adds 'a wip task stays resumable and closable', but the sentence before it still says that while the epic is blocked 'tp resume reports the block as a blocker and offers no implement unit, so tp run never drives a unit that cannot move', and that sentence has no wip exception. With a wip task and a regressed dependency, one implementation has tp resume offer the implement unit, since that unit can move. Another follows the literal sentence and offers none, so under tp run the WIP task stalls until the dependency converges again. That second outcome is the one the finding described. Row 3 does not settle it: its tp resume check runs on two open tasks with no wip, and for the wip task it checks only that the task is 'closable'.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md:94-98 lists the four commands and 'the block applies to starting the next one'; skills/tp/SKILL.md:775 '`tp done` auto-claims open tasks — no separate `tp claim` needed'; internal/cli/done.go:193-194 '// Implicit claim: open -> wip -> done / if task.Status == model.StatusOpen'; done.go:332-364 computes readyCount from DependsOn only and returns "has_next": readyCount > 0.
finding: §6 lists the gated entry points as `tp next`, `tp next --peek`, `tp ready` and `tp claim`, and adds that 'the block applies to starting the next one'. `tp done` also starts tasks: called on an open task it claims it implicitly (open → wip → done), and it checks only the task's own `depends_on`. So on a blocked file, `tp done <open-id>` starts and closes a task the block exists to hold back. The same code reports `remaining.ready` and `has_next: true` from task dependencies alone, so closing the in-flight wip task tells the agent there is a next task that `tp next` will not give it. An implementer who gates only the listed commands leaves both holes; one who follows 'the block applies to starting' closes them. The spec does not say which.

finding: The `TP_UNATTENDED` fence covers 'a binding written by `tp init --epic` or `tp set --epic`'. It is unclear whether removing a binding (`tp set --epic ""`, §2) counts as a binding written. If it does not, an unattended unit that hits `blocked_by_epics` can unbind its file, and §6 then lets every task through ('An unbound file behaves as it does at `v1.4.2`'). That defeats the block §6 adds so that `tp run` never drives work the graph holds back, and it moves the epic's status from `specced`/`in_progress` to `planned`, which is the operator's decision about starting it. Two correct implementations would disagree on whether `--epic ""` exits 2.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md:123-127: 'a done epic cuts a chain ... The heaviest such chain by summed estimate is reported only when every not-done epic the gate's members depend on has an estimate'
finding: The condition for reporting the estimate-weighted chain, 'every not-done epic the gate's members depend on has an estimate', can be read two ways, and each gives a different result. (1) Does 'the gate's members depend on' include the not-done members themselves? Every chain ends at a member, so the sum needs the member's estimate, but the sentence names only the epics the members depend on. (2) Is the dependency followed past a done epic? §7 says 'a done epic cuts a chain', so a not-done epic behind a done one is on no chain. Read transitively, though, the members still 'depend on' it. Take a→b→c with gate member a not done, b done, and c not done with no estimate: one implementation suppresses the weighted chain because of c, the other reports [a]. Likewise, if a has no estimate, one implementation reports a sum that leaves a out and the other reports nothing.
